description.en: Five lessons on case-control and cohort studies: forming a hypothesis, choosing a design, odds and risk ratios, bias, and measuring risk over time.

question.en: Who are you in this course, and what case will you work on?

title.en: A hunch is not yet a claim

question.en: When does a hunch become a claim that a study can test?

misconception.en: Taking a hunch such as "thalidomide causes birth defects" for a finding. A study can test a claim only when it names the people, the cause, the outcome, the dose and the time.

title.en: A comparison is only as fair as its controls

question.en: Whom do you compare the cases with, so that the comparison is fair?

misconception.en: Thinking that any group without the disease will do as controls. Controls taken from other hospital patients can share the exposure and hide a real effect; they must come from the same people the cases came from.

title.en: A case-control table gives odds, not risk

question.en: What does a case-control table measure, and how strongly?

misconception.en: Reading "33 of 35 lung-cancer patients smoked" (94 per cent) as a smoker's 94 per cent chance of lung cancer. A case-control table gives the odds of exposure, so it yields an odds ratio, never a risk.

title.en: A big ratio can be manufactured

question.en: Could the way the study was run have built that number?

misconception.en: Believing that a large ratio must be a real effect. The way cases and controls are chosen and asked, for example a hospital-only sample or an interviewer who knows who is ill, can build a large ratio on its own. Check for bias before trusting it.

title.en: Follow them forward and measure the risk

question.en: How do you measure the risk itself, and does it agree with the odds ratio?

misconception.en: Treating the odds ratio and the relative risk as the same measure, or calling every "retrospective" study a case-control study. Only a cohort, which runs from exposure to disease, measures incidence and so gives the relative risk.
